Quiz – lessons from the pile builder
What holds the wall of a CFA bore during drilling?
Nothing – the bore stands by itself
The soil remaining on the continuous auger supports the wall, so CFA needs no separate support.
In profile A (soft clay over gravel) you lengthen the 13 m CFA pile to 20 m. What happens?
The share of the shaft increases, and the “end-bearing” pile becomes mixed
The share of the base increases, it becomes even more end-bearing
Nothing, because the base is in the same layer
It becomes a friction pile, because the base gets into a soft layer
The longer shaft running in the bearing stratum takes an ever larger share – the share of the base falls below 2/3.
Why is a driven precast pile risky on a city-centre infill site?
Driving causes significant noise and vibration
Because concreting is impossible below the groundwater
Because it does not compact the soil
Because it can be at most 4 m long
The dynamic effect of driving also reaches the neighbouring buildings – near structures it can only be used under strict limits.
In cased drilling below the groundwater, what must be done in the bore?
Replace the water removed, so that the soil does not break in at the base
Pump out the water so that the base is dry
Grout the base with cement
Nothing, the casing solves everything
If the water level inside falls below that outside, the water pressure difference breaks in and loosens the soil at the base.
For which is the tip resistance neglected when calculating the resistance?
Driven precast pile
For a slender micropile typically only the shaft resistance is taken into account.
A widened base rammed out of batches of concrete
The excess concrete left above the pile head
A steel shoe welded onto the end of the casing
The top layer of concrete mixed with slurry
After the plug is driven out, further batches of concrete are rammed at the base – this “bulb” gives the high base resistance.
Hard clay, the groundwater is deep, an 8 m bored pile is needed. What is the simplest support?
No support – but it must be concreted immediately
A casing with water replacement
Compressed air
In cohesive soil above the groundwater, the bore stands by itself for a short time to at most 8–10 m.
For a cast-in-place screw pile, which resistance does the displacement mainly increase?
The shaft resistance
Only the base resistance
It reduces the shaft resistance
The head pushes aside and compacts the soil around the pile – this acts along the shaft.
A deep foundation can transfer load to the soil not only at its lower bearing surface (base) but also along its side, its shaft.
That is why it is a load-transferring element: its resistance is the sum of the base (tip) and the shaft resistance.
For a mixed (combined) pile both the tip and the shaft resistance contribute between 33 and 66 % of the resistance.
If neither reaches 2/3, the pile acts as a mixed pile.
If at least 2/3 of the resistance comes from the shaft, we speak of an end-bearing pile.
That is the friction pile. For an end-bearing pile at least 2/3 of the resistance is tip resistance: the pile “stands” in a layer of much better bearing capacity.
When anchoring against uplift – for example for underground car parks and tanks – the pile works as a tension element.
A pile can also go into tension if a pile group receives a large eccentric load.
A tension pile transfers its load to the soil through the base and the shaft together.
In a tension pile only the shaft works, in the opposite direction to the compression case.
Piles with a diameter greater than 80 cm are typically precast and installed with displacement technology.
Large-diameter piles are made exclusively with replacement technology.
For river piers of bridges, a shallow foundation is the safest solution because of the risk of scour.
Exactly the opposite: the risk of scour is one of the typical reasons for a deep foundation – as is the risk of sliding or settlement that a shallow foundation would make unacceptable.
A replacement pile is always cast in place.
The soil is removed (bored out) and the resulting hole is filled; meanwhile the surrounding soil may loosen slightly.
For a precast pile installed into the ground, the displacement increases both the base and the shaft resistance.
For a cast-in-place screw pile mainly the shaft resistance increases.
A cast-in-place screw pile brings the soil up while drilling, so a lot of spoil has to be removed.
The displacement drilling head pushes aside and compacts the soil; only a little spoil comes to the surface.
Pile driving can be used without problems even in hard clay and fill with large blocks.
It cannot be used in rock, hard clay, strongly cemented soil or blocky fill – even a thin such intercalation can prevent it.
Ground screws are typically 10–15 m long and are for founding heavily loaded bridges.
They are typically at most 2–3 m long, for lightly loaded structures: lightweight houses, solar parks, fences, mobile stands.
In vibration, by tuning the frequency to the natural frequency of the soil, the soil resistance can be temporarily reduced to a minimum.
Vibration is used mainly in granular soil; the loud noise is reduced by screening.
At the base of a Franki pile a widened concrete base, the “bulb”, is formed by ramming.
The compacted concrete base greatly increases the bearing capacity (2000–3000 kN can be achieved).
Loosened, settled or collapsed soil remaining at the bottom of the bore can greatly reduce the tip resistance of the pile.
That is why the pile base must be cleaned before concreting.
The casing of a Franki pile is driven down with hammer blows on the top of the tube.
The approx. 1 m dry concrete plug placed in the tube is rammed with a 3 t drop hammer, and the concrete drags the tube down with it through friction.
The short auger is used mainly in granular soil, the drilling bucket mainly in cohesive soil.
The other way round: the short auger is mainly for cohesive soil and the drilling bucket mainly for granular soil; the grab and the continuous auger work in any soil.
The concrete of a CFA pile must be vibrated thoroughly after it is placed in the bore.
No vibration is needed: the flowing consistency and placing under pressure ensure self-compaction.
For a CFA pile the wall of the bore is supported by the soil plug remaining on the auger; no separate support is needed.
This is one of the biggest advantages of the continuous auger.
That is why the pile is usually concreted up to the working level.
In cased drilling below the groundwater, the water removed must be replaced in the bore, otherwise groundwater may break in at the base.
The higher water level outside would disturb the soil with water breaking in at the bottom of the bore.
The typical length of a CFA pile is 30–50 m.
It is typically 6–22 (24) m long and 40–120 cm in diameter.
In granular soil the casing goes down after the excavation, lagging behind it.
The casing must generally – in granular soil without exception – go ahead of the excavation.
For a bentonite-supported pile the concrete is dropped freely from the top into the slurry-filled bore.
Concreting is done through a tremie pipe, from the bottom up; the concrete displaces the slurry.
In cohesive soil above the groundwater, a bore at most 8–10 m deep can be made without support, but it must be concreted immediately.
Up to a depth of 5–6 m such a foundation is also called an excavated block foundation or well foundation.
The shaft diameter of a bored micropile is 400–600 mm.
Bored micropile: at most 250–300 mm; driven micropile: at most 150 mm.
For a micropile, buckling must be checked separately if the undrained shear strength of the soil layer is less than 10 kPa.
Because of the small diameter, the slender pile can buckle in soft soil.
When calculating the resistance of a micropile, the base resistance is neglected.
The shaft resistance is determined by the method of construction, so a load test is justified.
In jet grouting the cement suspension is injected into the soil at a pressure of 5–6 bar.
The pressure of the grout jet is 400–600 bar; 5–6 bar is the pressure of the air shroud in the double jet with air.
A diaphragm wall panel can be excavated in one go as long as 30 m.
A panel is at most 8–10 m, typically 2.8–5.6 m long – this is set by trench stability.
For a CFA pile the reinforcement cage is lowered into the freshly concreted pile.
